title: Pruned Pathways
question: During adolescence the human brain eliminates many unused synaptic connections while strengthening frequently used ones, and this pruning is a normal part of healthy development.
correctExplanation: True. Developmental pruning removes weak synapses and keeps efficient circuits, which is why teenage brains remodel rather than simply grow.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. Pruning is construction through subtraction: unused connections are cleared while active ones stabilize. The process refines networks instead of signaling damage.
lessonContent:
Plasticity includes both growth and well-timed removal of connections.
Use preserves circuits while neglect marks them for pruning.
Adolescence remodels networks toward adult efficiency.
More synapses do not always mean better function.
Share this: explain tonight why forgetting unused routes can make a network smarter.

title: Ten Percent Myth
question: Humans normally use only about ten percent of their brains in daily life, leaving the remaining ninety percent dormant and waiting to be unlocked.
correctExplanation: False. Brain imaging shows virtually all regions active across a day, with different networks engaging for different tasks.
incorrectExplanation: It is false. Scans reveal no large dormant reserve sitting idle. Damage to almost any area causes deficits, which would be impossible if ninety percent did nothing.
lessonContent:
Popular brain myths often promise hidden reserves without evidence.
Modern imaging tracks activity across the whole organ during ordinary days.
Selective activation is efficiency, not idleness.
A claim that flatters the listener deserves extra skepticism.
Share this: ask someone where they first heard the ten-percent claim and check its source.

title: Newborn Neurons
question: In adult humans, new neurons continue to form in the hippocampus, a brain region central to learning and memory.
correctExplanation: True. Evidence supports ongoing hippocampal neurogenesis in adults, where newborn cells gradually integrate into memory circuits.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. The adult brain is not entirely fixed in cell number. Hippocampal newborn neurons take weeks to mature and then participate in forming new memories.
lessonContent:
Some brain regions retain a capacity for generating new neurons.
New cells need time, activity, and survival signals to integrate.
Learning and exercise influence whether newborn cells persist.
Plasticity spans synapses, maps, and in limited regions new cells.
Share this: name one hippocampus-dependent skill you practiced this month.

title: Sleep Files Memories
question: Sleep after learning helps stabilize new memories, so material followed by sleep is typically recalled better than the same material followed by staying awake.
correctExplanation: True. Sleep supports consolidation: replay and restructuring during rest strengthen fragile traces into durable ones.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. Study-sleep-test designs repeatedly favor the sleep condition. Rest does active work, replaying patterns and integrating them with older knowledge.
lessonContent:
Consolidation continues after practice ends.
Sleep replay lets fragile traces stabilize and connect.
Timing study before rest can protect new learning.
Rest is part of training, not its opposite.
Share this: schedule one study session to finish before sleep this week.

title: Wanting Versus Liking
question: Dopamine mainly produces the feeling of pleasure itself, so raising dopamine always increases how much someone enjoys a reward.
correctExplanation: False. Dopamine drives wanting and motivation more than liking; pleasure itself depends on additional systems.
incorrectExplanation: It is false. Experiments separate pursuit from enjoyment: dopamine-depleted animals still show liking reactions but stop working for rewards. Craving and pleasure are distinct circuits.
lessonContent:
Motivation and pleasure run on partly separate machinery.
Wanting pushes pursuit while liking registers enjoyment.
Confusing the two misreads cravings as happiness.
Labels like pleasure chemical oversimplify careful findings.
Share this: notice one craving today and ask whether it promises wanting or liking.

title: Costly Task Switching
question: Rapidly alternating between two demanding tasks is just as efficient as completing each in turn, because attention divides between tasks without any cost.
correctExplanation: False. Switching imposes measurable costs in time and errors as the brain reconfigures goals and rules.
incorrectExplanation: It is false. What feels like parallel work is rapid serial switching. Each switch pays a reconfiguration toll, so heavy multitasking slows both tasks and raises mistakes.
lessonContent:
Attention is a limited resource that must be reallocated.
Switch costs appear in slower responses and extra errors.
Single-tasking protects demanding reasoning from interruption.
Feeling busy is not evidence of thinking well.
Share this: time one task with and without phone interruptions today.

title: Locked After Childhood
question: Once early childhood critical periods close, the adult brain cannot reorganize at all, which makes any recovery of lost function impossible.
correctExplanation: False. Adult plasticity is reduced in some domains but remains real, and rehabilitation routinely drives partial recovery.
incorrectExplanation: It is false. Critical periods set sensitivities, not padlocks. Adult maps remap after injury and training, which is the entire basis of modern neurorehabilitation.
lessonContent:
Critical periods shape timing without ending all change.
Adult reorganization is slower and more effortful, yet genuine.
Training dose and specificity decide much of the outcome.
Absolutes like never and impossible misdescribe biology.
Share this: describe one adult skill you watched someone rebuild through practice.

title: Exercise Feeds Memory
question: Regular aerobic exercise is associated with higher levels of brain growth factors and with better memory performance in older adults.
correctExplanation: True. Trials link sustained aerobic activity to growth-factor signaling and to measurable gains in hippocampus-dependent memory.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. The effect is association plus converging trial evidence, not magic. Movement supports the chemistry that plasticity runs on, especially in aging brains.
lessonContent:
The body supplies conditions the brain remodels within.
Aerobic habits correlate with healthier memory aging.
Growth factors translate activity into synaptic support.
Small sustained doses beat rare heroic workouts.
Share this: take one brisk walk today and treat it as memory training.

title: Recovery Through Rewiring
question: After a stroke, intensive rehabilitation can recruit undamaged brain areas to take over functions once handled by damaged tissue.
correctExplanation: True. Constraint and task-specific training push surviving networks to reorganize and assume impaired roles.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. Recovery is not only swelling subsiding. Imaging shows neighboring and connected regions changing their responses as patients regain movement and language.
lessonContent:
Rehabilitation is applied plasticity with a schedule.
Specific, repeated, challenging practice drives remapping.
Spared tissue can learn jobs it never held before.
Dose and difficulty matter more than vague encouragement.
Share this: explain why rehab exercises repeat one movement hundreds of times.

title: Phantom Map Shift
question: In some arm amputees, touch on the face is felt as coming from the missing hand, because neighboring cortical maps expand after losing their normal input.
correctExplanation: True. Face and hand zones sit adjacently in cortex, so deprived hand territory gets invaded by face inputs.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. The mislocation follows the cortical map, not the skin. Neighboring representations compete for deprived territory, which reveals how dynamically maps are maintained.
lessonContent:
Cortical maps are maintained by competition between inputs.
Losing input lets neighbors expand into silent territory.
Felt location follows brain mapping, not just skin site.
Remapping explains both phantom sensations and recovery.
Share this: sketch the cortical homunculus and find the hand-face border.

title: Memory Update Window
question: Briefly recalling an established memory can make it temporarily malleable, so new information presented in that window can update the stored trace.
correctExplanation: True. Recalled traces enter a labile reconsolidation phase before stabilizing again, admitting targeted updates.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. Retrieval does not merely read a file. The reactivated trace must restabilize, and interference or new learning during that window reshapes what persists.
lessonContent:
Retrieval opens memories to editing, not just replay.
Labile windows close as traces restabilize.
Update beats erasure as a model of memory change.
Therapy and teaching can exploit restabilization deliberately.
Share this: recall one memory today and notice which details feel reconstructed.

title: Spacing Beats Cramming
question: Spreading study sessions across several days produces stronger long-term retention than massing the same total study hours into a single night.
correctExplanation: True. Distributed practice consistently outperforms massed practice on delayed tests across subjects and ages.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. Cramming inflates immediate familiarity while spacing builds durable retrieval routes. The advantage grows as the test delay lengthens.
lessonContent:
Timing of practice matters as much as total hours.
Spacing forces effortful reconstruction that strengthens traces.
Immediate fluency is a poor predictor of lasting recall.
Plan review at expanding intervals for durable learning.
Share this: split your next study topic into three short sessions.

title: Testing Beats Rereading
question: Actively retrieving information during practice strengthens later recall more than spending the same time simply rereading the material.
correctExplanation: True. The testing effect shows retrieval practice builds stronger memories than restudying, even when practice feels harder.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. Rereading raises fluency without building access routes. Effortful recall modifies the trace itself, which is why self-quizzing wins on delayed tests.
lessonContent:
Retrieval is a memory modifier, not just a measurement.
Difficulty during practice often predicts durability later.
Self-testing exposes gaps that rereading hides.
Low-stakes quizzes convert study time into recall strength.
Share this: close the book and recall its points before rereading anything.

title: Stress Sharpens Everything
question: Acute severe stress improves every kind of thinking equally, including flexible reasoning, working memory, and creative problem solving.
correctExplanation: False. Severe stress typically impairs prefrontal flexibility and working memory while favoring rigid habit responses.
incorrectExplanation: It is false. Stress hormones retune the brain toward fast defensive routines. Simple well-drilled actions may survive, but deliberation and mental juggling reliably suffer.
lessonContent:
Arousal reshapes which systems control behavior.
Moderate pressure can focus simple tasks and wreck complex ones.
Habit circuits gain influence as flexible planning degrades.
One lever rarely moves every ability in the same direction.
Share this: notice which thinking style your next deadline strengthens or weakens.

title: Repurposed Visual Cortex
question: People blind from an early age often recruit visual cortex for hearing and touch tasks, demonstrating cross-modal reorganization.
correctExplanation: True. Deprived visual areas get colonized by other senses, and disrupting them impairs Braille reading and sound localization.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. Cortex is less strictly single-purpose than textbook labels imply. When vision never arrives, remaining senses bid for the unused computational territory.
lessonContent:
Cortical territory follows input, not just labels.
Deprivation invites takeover by surviving senses.
Function follows connectivity more than anatomy names.
The brain reassigns hardware before wasting it.
Share this: describe blindness as reassignment rather than a switched-off module.

title: Cab Drivers Hippocampus
question: Experienced London taxi drivers who memorized the city's full street layout show structural differences in the hippocampus compared with matched controls.
correctExplanation: True. Navigation expertise correlates with hippocampal differences that grow with years of demanding spatial practice.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. Memorizing thousands of routes is years of spatial training. The associated structural pattern supports experience shaping the adult brain rather than talent alone explaining performance.
lessonContent:
Sustained expertise leaves structural traces.
Spatial memory taxes the hippocampus heavily.
Years of practice, not weeks, produce the clearest changes.
Correlation invites training studies before claiming causation.
Share this: navigate one familiar route from memory without assistance today.

title: Enriched Cages
question: Rats raised in complex stimulating environments develop denser synaptic connections than rats raised in bare isolated cages.
correctExplanation: True. Enrichment studies show thicker cortex and richer connectivity in animals given novelty, company, and activity.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. The differences survive controls for handling and exercise. An impoverished environment is itself an intervention that shrinks what a normal one would build.
lessonContent:
Environment sculpts synaptic density measurably.
Novelty, social life, and movement each contribute.
Control conditions decide what counts as baseline.
Deprivation studies reveal what stimulation normally builds.
Share this: add one novel demanding activity to your week as enrichment.

title: Fixed White Matter
question: Only gray matter changes with learning, while the brain's white-matter pathways are permanently fixed after childhood and never remodel.
correctExplanation: False. White matter shows experience-dependent change too, including myelin remodeling that tunes conduction speed.
incorrectExplanation: It is false. Imaging of musicians, jugglers, and readers finds white-matter differences tied to practice. Insulation as well as wiring adapts to demand.
lessonContent:
Learning tunes transmission, not only computation.
Myelin adjusts speed and synchrony along used routes.
Both gray and white matter participate in skill.
Fixed-versus-plastic framings usually collapse under data.
Share this: think of practice as upgrading cables as well as processors.

title: Juggling Grows Cortex
question: Months of juggling practice can produce measurable gray-matter changes in visual motion areas, which recede after practice stops.
correctExplanation: True. Training studies found transient gray-matter expansion tied to juggling that diminished with detraining.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. The rise-and-fall pattern links the change to practice itself. Brains expand the machinery a skill needs and release it when demand ends.
lessonContent:
Structural change can be rapid and reversible.
New skills rent cortical space while they are needed.
Detraining reversals strengthen causal interpretation.
Short studies can reveal what lifelong data only suggest.
Share this: practice one coordination skill daily for two weeks and track progress.

title: Video Recorder Memory
question: Human memory works like a video recorder, storing exact copies of events that replay unchanged every time they are recalled.
correctExplanation: False. Memory is reconstructive: each recall rebuilds the event from fragments and current context, introducing distortions.
incorrectExplanation: It is false. Confidence predicts accuracy poorly because recall reassembles rather than replays. Misinformation and leading questions demonstrably rewrite details.
lessonContent:
Recall reconstructs instead of replaying.
Fragments plus expectations assemble each remembering.
Confidence is a feeling, not a fidelity meter.
External records beat vivid recollection for accuracy.
Share this: compare your memory of one event with a photo or message record.

title: Limits of Attention
question: Conscious attention has no meaningful capacity limit, so a person focused on one demanding task is guaranteed to notice any unexpected object nearby.
correctExplanation: False. Inattentional blindness shows focused observers can miss even conspicuous unexpected events in plain view.
incorrectExplanation: It is false. The famous invisible-gorilla studies prove missing the obvious while counting passes. Attention selects, and selection necessarily discards the rest.
lessonContent:
Seeing requires attention as well as open eyes.
Focused tasks filter supposedly obvious surroundings.
No observer catches everything in a scene.
Design for limits instead of denying them.
Share this: watch a familiar walk once for something you never noticed.

title: Shock Therapy Myth
question: Modern electroconvulsive therapy improves severe depression by destroying large areas of brain tissue, with no involvement of plasticity mechanisms.
correctExplanation: False. Modern ECT is controlled and does not lesion tissue; its benefits are linked to seizure-related plasticity and growth-factor signaling.
incorrectExplanation: It is false. Imaging shows no large-scale destruction, while markers of plasticity rise after treatment. The historical brutality narrative misdescribes the regulated modern procedure.
lessonContent:
Effective treatments can work through plasticity, not damage.
Mechanism claims need tissue-level evidence.
History colors perception of modern procedures.
Separate past misuse from current controlled practice.
Share this: replace one movie-myth treatment claim with its measured evidence.

title: Musicians Finger Maps
question: String players show enlarged cortical representation for the fingers of their fretting hand compared with people who do not play such instruments.
correctExplanation: True. Intensive left-hand fingering expands its sensory maps, with the effect strongest in early starters.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. Thousands of hours of precise finger work reshape sensory cortex. Map size follows practice history rather than musical talent alone.
lessonContent:
Repetition with precision expands sensory maps.
Starting age and practice hours both predict map size.
Skill lives partly in reorganized perception.
Practice writes itself into the sensing brain.
Share this: compare fingertip sensitivity across your own two hands.

title: Game Boosts Everything
question: Playing one commercial brain-training game for a few hours permanently raises general intelligence across all unrelated tasks.
correctExplanation: False. Training improves the trained task and close neighbors, but far transfer to general intelligence is weak or absent.
incorrectExplanation: It is false. Reviews find near transfer without broad gains. Getting better at a game mostly means getting better at that game, not upgrading the whole mind.
lessonContent:
Transfer is narrow unless training shares real demands.
Near gains do not imply general upgrades.
Marketing leaps from task scores to intelligence claims.
Judge programs by independent untrained measures.
Share this: test any brain claim by asking what untrained skill improved.

title: Mozart Effect Promise
question: Having infants listen to classical music for a few minutes permanently raises their intelligence lasting into adulthood.
correctExplanation: False. The original finding was a brief spatial-task boost in adults, not a lasting intelligence increase in babies.
incorrectExplanation: It is false. Short arousal effects were inflated into permanent genius claims. Follow-ups find no enduring IQ gain from passive listening sessions.
lessonContent:
Brief performance lifts differ from lasting ability change.
Arousal and mood explain many music-listening boosts.
Extraordinary claims need longitudinal evidence.
Enrichment means engagement, not background audio.
Share this: swap passive listening for active music-making with a child.
